claims.text: The initial material is a multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy with established phase boundaries and a stable interphase microstructure.
Exposure around 500–600 °C can activate dynamic precipitation in the target alloy.
Exposure around 500–600 °C can activate dynamic recrystallization in the target alloy.
The dynamically formed precipitates can be carbide-like or Cr-rich σ-phase-like features.
Dynamic precipitates form along phase boundaries in the multiphase eutectic alloy.
Dynamic precipitation and recrystallization create brittle or mechanically weak interfacial regions.
The interfacial precipitates act as localized cathodic or galvanic sites.
The precipitates reduce the alloy's resistance to mechanical abrasion.
Wear preferentially removes or disrupts precipitates located at interfacial regions.
Preferential interfacial removal exposes fresh, defect-rich, chemically active surfaces.
The freshly exposed defect-rich surfaces corrode more rapidly through galvanic coupling.
Mechanical removal and chemical attack form a positive feedback that produces degradation beyond the additive effects of separate wear and corrosion.
Combined wear and corrosion will produce total degradation greater than the sum of the wear-only and corrosion-only responses.
Combined exposure will produce a higher wear volume than wear-only exposure because of premature interfacial failure.
Combined exposure will produce a higher corrosion rate than corrosion-only exposure because of increased active surface area and galvanic effects.
The proposed mechanism requires a sufficiently aggressive corrosive environment together with mechanical wear.
Separate wear-only and corrosion-only tests at the same temperature, loading duration, and exposure duration provide baselines for testing degradation synergy.
Preferential precipitate removal and interfacial degradation can be assessed by SEM or TEM characterization.
